habitat: Wild from Newfoundland and Manitoba through the Great Lakes and New England, and south along the Appalachians to northern Georgia. It grows on almost any soil, but competes best on well-drained sands and gravels, where it once formed vast stands; it also takes rocky ridges and the edges of bogs. Young trees grow well in partial shade.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the central United States, from Pennsylvania west to South Dakota and south to Texas, mostly on the rich, moist bottomlands of river valleys and on limestone soils. Planted, it puts up with drought, road salt, compacted soil and city heat, which is how it reached northern streets.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The most widespread oak of the Northeast, from Nova Scotia and the Great Lakes south to Alabama and west to Minnesota and eastern Oklahoma. It grows best on deep, moist, well-drained loams on north- and east-facing slopes and in coves, but is common on drier ridges too. Its seedlings stand moderate shade and shoot up when a gap opens in the canopy.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild along rivers, streams and the edges of swamps in the eastern and central United States, from southern New England and New York to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas, on ground that floods in spring. It needs sun, and acid soil: on alkaline ground its leaves turn yellow.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across much of Europe, from Norway and Finland south to northern Spain and Greece and east to the Caucasus, in mixed forests on rich, moist soils, seldom in stands of its own. In North American woods its seedlings stand deep shade, and come up thickly under its own crown.

A tree of wet ground: river bottoms, the edges of swamps and lakes, and flats that flood in spring, from southern Quebec and Maine west to Minnesota and south to Missouri and Virginia, scattered among other trees rather than in stands. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the lowland forests of the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild only in the central and southern Rocky Mountains, from Wyoming and Idaho to New Mexico and Arizona, mostly along streams and on moist slopes in mountain valleys between about 6,000 and 11,000 feet, seldom in stands of its own. Planted, it does best in full sun and well-drained soil.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: It grows on a wider range of ground than almost any other tree in eastern North America: swamps and stream banks, dry rocky ridges and everything between, in sun or part shade, from Newfoundland to Florida and west to Minnesota and eastern Texas.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in scattered mountain ranges of southern Europe and Asia Minor, from Spain and Corsica through Austria and the Balkans to Crimea and Turkey, often on limestone and on poor, dry, rocky soils where few other trees do well.

Wild on poorly drained bottomlands and flats that stand in water through winter and spring, from southern New England and New York west to Iowa and Kansas and south to Tennessee and North Carolina. It needs acid soil, and grows fast in full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec west to Minnesota and south to Tennessee, and along the Appalachians to Georgia. At its best on deep, moist, fertile, well-drained loams, where it often dominates the forest with beech and yellow birch. Its seedlings stand deep shade and can wait decades under the canopy for a gap.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and the St. Lawrence west to Manitoba, and south through the Great Lakes states and New England, with scattered outliers in the Appalachians. It grows in two very different places: cedar swamps on wet, often limy peat, and dry limestone ledges and cliffs.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: One of the most widespread trees in North America: across the northern forest from Newfoundland and Labrador to Alaska, and south to the Great Lakes, northern New England and the Adirondacks. It grows on a wide range of soils, best on moist, well-drained loams, and stands bitter cold.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, from England and Spain east to the Urals and the Caucasus, in mixed broadleaf forests on fertile soils. In England it is a mark of ancient woodland, where it has grown since before people cleared the land.

Wild in the mountains of central and southeastern Europe, up to about 2,000 m in the Alps, and across the lowlands of Scandinavia and northern Russia, where it forms vast forests on cool, moist soils.
Wild in Japan, Korea, eastern China and Taiwan, along streams and in moist valleys on rich soils.

Almost every ginkgo alive was planted. Whether any truly wild ones remain is debated: the likeliest are scattered trees in the mountains of southwestern China, which some think were kept alive by Buddhist monks for centuries.

Wild from New Brunswick west to Manitoba and south to Arkansas and the mountains of North Carolina, on moist, deep, fertile soils of slopes and valleys. It grows mixed with sugar maple, elms and ashes rather than in stands, and sprouts readily from a cut stump.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: A tree of riverbanks and floodplains, from New Brunswick west to Minnesota and south to Louisiana and Georgia, where it stands spring floods for weeks. In Vermont it dominates the floodplain forests along the big rivers and the shores of Lake Champlain.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the northern forest from Newfoundland to Alaska, south to Pennsylvania and the Great Lakes. A pioneer: it seeds into ground opened by fire, logging or clearing, in full sun, and gives way in time to trees that stand more shade.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Quebec and Maine west to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, along streams, in bottomlands and on rich lower slopes, in the shade of taller hardwoods. It stands more shade than almost any tree it grows among.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Native to the eastern United States, chiefly the Southeast and the lower Midwest, at forest edges, in old fields and thickets and in young woods coming back on cleared land. In New England, Vermont included, it grows only where planted.
Wild in northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido, and in Korea, northern China and the far southeast of Russia, in mixed forests, valleys and gullies from near sea level into the mountains.

Wild from southern Maine west to Iowa and Nebraska and south to northern Florida and Texas, almost always on bottomlands and along streams, where it grows faster than nearly any hardwood. It is often among the first trees on new ground left by a river.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Its original range is not known exactly: two separate areas, one in the Appalachians from Pennsylvania and southern Ohio to Alabama and Georgia, the other in the Ozarks and Ouachita Mountains of Missouri, Arkansas and Oklahoma. Planted for posts and erosion control, it has since run wild across the country and into Europe and Asia, on open, disturbed ground in full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild only in a few mountain ranges of the Balkans: mainly the Pindus of Greece, with small stands in North Macedonia, Albania and Bulgaria, in moist, shaded ravines and valley forests. The trees of streets and parks across Europe and North America all descend from planted ones.
source: European Atlas of Forest Tree Species (European Commission)

habitat: Wild across most of Europe, from Ireland and Portugal east to the Urals and the Caucasus, at its best on deep, moist, fertile soils, including heavy clays and river floodplains. It needs sun: its seedlings fail under a closed canopy.

Wild on the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from Delaware to Florida and Texas, and up the Mississippi valley to southern Illinois and Indiana, in swamps, river bottoms and lake edges that stand in water for much of the year. Planted in the open it does well on ordinary soil, and is hardy far north of where it grows wild.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the central and northern plains and the Midwest, from southern Manitoba and New Brunswick south to Texas, farther west than any other eastern oak: on river bottoms, dry uplands and the savannas between forest and prairie, where its thick bark let it survive the grass fires that kept other trees out. In Vermont it grows wild in the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountains of northern Japan, mostly Hokkaido and northern Honshu, and in Korea, Sakhalin, the Kuril Islands and the far southeast of Russia: the coldest homeland of any of the ornamental cherries.
source: Plants of the World Online (Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew)

habitat: A cultivated form that grows wild nowhere, kept going from cuttings. Its species, the black poplar, grows wild along rivers and on floodplains from Europe to central Asia, on wet sand and gravel that floods.

Native to a small area of the central Mississippi valley, from southern Illinois and Indiana to Arkansas and western Tennessee, in bottomland woods along streams and at the foot of bluffs. Planted far beyond that for its flowers and fast growth, it has run wild in old fields and along fencerows across much of the East.

Before the blight it was among the commonest trees of the Appalachian forest, from Maine and southern Ontario to Georgia and Mississippi, above all on well-drained, acid soils of ridges and upper slopes. It survives there now mostly as sprouts from old root systems.

Wild in two forms: the coast Douglas fir, from British Columbia to central California, among the tallest trees in the world; and the smaller, hardier Rocky Mountain Douglas fir, from Alberta to Mexico. The trees planted in the Northeast are mostly the inland form, which stands cold winters.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Scotland and Spain across Europe and northern Asia to eastern Siberia, and north beyond the Arctic Circle in Scandinavia. It grows on a wide range of soils, including dry sands and poor, rocky ground where little else does well, but needs full sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Scattered through the hardwood forests of the East and Midwest, from western Vermont and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, rarely in stands of its own. It grows best on deep, rich, moist but well-drained bottomlands and coves, and needs sun.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Michigan and New Jersey south to Florida, and west to Texas and northern Mexico, mostly as a small understory tree of open woods, woodland edges, rocky slopes and stream banks.
source: Fire Effects Information System (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild through almost the whole of the eastern United States, from southern Maine and Quebec west to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, on many kinds of ground but best on deep, moist, well-drained soils. It is long-lived, slow-growing and moderately shade-tolerant.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and the Great Lakes south along the Appalachians to Georgia and Alabama, in cool, moist places: ravines, north-facing slopes, stream banks and rocky ridges. It stands more shade than almost any other tree in its range.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern New England and southern Ontario west to Michigan and south to Florida and Louisiana, at its best in the deep, moist, well-drained soils of Appalachian coves and lower slopes. It grows fast and needs sun, so it fills gaps and old fields. In Vermont it is rare.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from Hungary and the Balkans to western Turkey, in mixed broadleaf forests on lowlands and hills. Its tolerance of heat and dry summers comes from there.

Wild only in a small area of central China, on the borders of Hubei, Hunan and Chongqing, in valleys and along streams in the mountains, mostly in or beside rice paddies and villages. Very few of the wild trees remain.

Wild from Connecticut and southern Illinois south to Florida and Texas, with scattered stands in the mountains of Mexico and Central America. A tree of bottomlands and moist slopes, it also seeds fast into old fields and cutover land.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Across the East from Nova Scotia and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, on rich, moist, well-drained soils, often with sugar maple and yellow birch in the northern hardwood forest. It stands deep shade, and spreads by suckers from its roots into thickets of young beech.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Europe across the Caucasus and the Himalaya to central China, on dry, rocky, sunny hillsides and in open woods, often on limestone.
Wild across most of Europe, north to southern Scandinavia, and in North Africa and western Asia, in woods, woodland edges and old hedgerows, on chalk and limestone as well as heavy clays.

An understory tree of dry, well-drained slopes and ridges across the East, from Nova Scotia and Manitoba to Florida and Texas, with stands in the mountains of Mexico and Central America. It grows slowly in the shade of oaks and maples.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild along the Pacific coast from southern Alaska to northern California, and inland in the Cascades, in cool, wet mountain forests, mostly at middle and upper elevations. It stands deep snow and poor, wet soils.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec west to Minnesota and south through the Appalachians, on sandy and gravelly uplands. It needs full sun and comes in fast after fire or cutting, mostly by suckers from the roots of the trees that were there.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the lower Midwest and the upper South, from Pennsylvania west to Kansas and south to Tennessee and Arkansas, on moist bottomlands and slopes, and in old fields and open woods.

Wild from Newfoundland and southern Quebec west to Minnesota, and south along the Appalachians to Georgia, on cool, moist, well-drained soils of slopes and stream banks, with sugar maple, beech and hemlock in the northern hardwood forest. Its seedlings take root on rotting logs and mossy stumps.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec to Pennsylvania and New Jersey, on poor, dry, sandy or gravelly ground and in abandoned fields, where it is among the first trees to come in after fire or clearing.
Wild in the eastern United States from New Jersey and Ohio south to Florida and Texas, as a small understory tree of moist woods, stream banks and the edges of swamps, and on dry rocky bluffs.
Wild in Japan and China, in moist forests along mountain streams, where old trees grow to great size, often with several trunks.

Wild across most of Europe, from southern England and Sweden to Sicily and the Balkans, forming forests of its own on well-drained soils, especially chalk and limestone. Its dense shade keeps almost anything else from growing beneath it.
Wild in China, Korea and Taiwan, in thickets, on forest edges and in mountain woods. Planted across North America, it has run wild in old fields, roadsides and woodland edges in much of the East.

Wild but scattered and nowhere common, from western New York and southern Ontario to Nebraska and Oklahoma, mostly on rich, moist bottomlands and lower slopes. It spreads by suckers, so a stand is often one tree's clones.
Wild in Japan, Korea and China, in mountain forests and thickets, as a small understory tree.
A cultivated tree, found wild only where it has escaped. Its main ancestor, the wild apple Malus sieversii, still grows in the mountain forests of Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan, in the Tian Shan.
Wild in the mountains of northeastern China and Korea, in mixed forests on slopes and along streams.

The most widespread maple in North America, wild from New England and southern Canada to Florida, California and Guatemala. A tree of riverbanks, floodplains and lake shores that also seeds fast into vacant lots, rail yards and old fields.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from West Virginia south to Florida and west to Arkansas and Oklahoma, along streams and on moist, rich slopes in coves.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, as an understory tree of open hardwood and pine forests, on moist, well-drained, acid soils. In Vermont it grows wild only in the south of the state.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Rare and scattered in the wild, in a few counties from Kentucky and Tennessee to Arkansas and Alabama, mostly on limestone cliffs, ridges and the rich soils of coves and stream banks.
Wild only in central China, in mixed forests on mountain slopes, where it is now rare.

Wild from southern Quebec and western Vermont to the Dakotas and south to Oklahoma and Georgia, most often on river bottoms and floodplains but also on dry, rocky limestone ridges. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in northeastern China, Korea, Japan and the Russian Far East, in mixed forests along rivers and on mountain slopes. Planted in the Northeast, it seeds into nearby woods.

The most widespread ash in North America, wild from Nova Scotia to Alberta and south to Florida and Texas, on moist bottomlands and stream banks. Planted along streets across the continent, it is now dying everywhere the emerald ash borer has reached.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountain forests of Japan and Korea, in moist, rich soils, often near streams.

Wild across almost all of Europe and northern Asia, from Iceland and Spain to Siberia, higher in the mountains than almost any other broadleaf tree. It grows on thin, acid soils, rocky ground and the edges of woods.

Across the northern forest from Labrador and Newfoundland to Alberta, south to the Great Lakes, northern New England and the Adirondacks, with outliers in the Appalachians. It grows on cool, moist ground from swamps to mountain slopes, and with red spruce makes up the dark forest of Vermont's higher mountains.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountains of the West, from Oregon and Idaho south through the Sierra Nevada and the Rockies to northern Mexico, on slopes at middle elevations. Its thick-barked, drought-hardened trees come from dry mountain slopes, which is why it copes with eastern summers.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec west to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, with stands in the mountains of Mexico and Central America. A tree of the northern hardwood forest at its best on the deep, moist soils of the Allegheny Plateau, it also seeds into old fields and fencerows, carried by birds.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Maine and New York south along the Appalachians to northern Georgia and Alabama, on moist, well-drained slopes and in coves, often with hemlock, sugar maple and yellow birch. In Vermont it grows wild mostly in the south and the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: A tree of southern river bottoms: wild on the floodplains and bottomland ridges of the coastal plain and the Mississippi valley, from New Jersey and southern Indiana to Florida and Texas, on ground that floods only briefly.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the mountains of central and southern Japan, in moist, cool forests on slopes, where it was long reserved for temples and palaces. It is still among the most planted timber trees in Japan.

Wild but scattered in the Southeast, from Ohio and Kentucky to Louisiana and Georgia, as an understory tree of rich, moist ravines and slopes, sheltered from the wind that would shred its huge leaves.

Wild in northern China, and grown across Asia for millennia to feed silkworms. Brought to North America for the same purpose, it has run wild in fencerows, vacant lots and woodland edges across the continent, and hybridizes with the native red mulberry.

Wild from southern Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and Texas, on ground that ranges from swamps and stream bottoms to dry ridges, scattered among other hardwoods rather than in stands. In Vermont it grows wild in a few swamps in the south of the state.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in Japan, Korea and eastern China, as a small understory tree of mountain forests, in the shade of taller trees along streams and on moist slopes.
Wild only in a few places in eastern China, in Zhejiang and Hubei, on rocky slopes and in thickets, where it is now rare.
Wild from Newfoundland and Nova Scotia west to Manitoba and south to the Great Lakes states, northern New England and Pennsylvania, on dry, sandy and gravelly soils, often in pure stands after fire.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the western Great Lakes region, from Michigan and Ontario to Minnesota and Iowa, on dry, sandy uplands and in oak savannas and open woods.
Wild across much of Europe, from southern England and France to Ukraine and Turkey, as an understory tree of oak and beech forests on moist, heavy soils.
Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans through Turkey to the Caucasus and northern Iran, in mixed mountain forests.

Wild across most of Europe, from Ireland and Scandinavia to the Urals, and in western Asia, mostly in hill and mountain woods on moist, fertile soils, often along streams. It reaches farther north and west than any other European elm.

Wild in western and central Asia, from Turkey and Iran to China, along rivers and in dry valleys. Planted in North America for windbreaks, it has run wild along streams and in grasslands of the West, and is marked invasive in Vermont.
Wild in the mountains around the Black Sea, in the western Caucasus and northeastern Turkey, in moist forests at middle and high elevations, often with oriental spruce and beech.

Wild across much of the eastern and central United States and into Mexico, from southern Ontario and New York to Florida and Arizona, at the edges of woods, on rocky slopes and dunes and along streams.
Wild in northeastern China, Korea and the Russian Far East, in mixed forests along rivers and on mountain slopes.

Wild from southern Maine and southern Ontario west to Iowa and south to Florida and Texas, in old fields, along fencerows and at woodland edges, where it spreads by suckers into thickets. In Vermont it grows wild only in the south of the state.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in southern and central Europe and western Asia, from France and Italy to the Caucasus, in open woods, thickets and woodland edges, often on limestone.

Wild on the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plains from Massachusetts to Florida and Texas, in swamps, bays and along streams, on wet, acid soils. In the north of its range it loses its leaves in winter; in the south it keeps them.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Probably not truly wild anywhere. It most likely arose as a hybrid around the Caspian and Black Seas, and grows across Europe, North Africa and western Asia where it has escaped from orchards.
Wild in the drier parts of northern China, from Inner Mongolia to Gansu and Shaanxi, and in Korea, along rivers and on open ground.
Wild in western and central Europe, from Britain to Spain and east to Poland: a shade-tolerant small tree of old woodland and ancient hedgerows on heavy clay soils.

Wild only in a narrow coastal strip about 750 km long, from the Chetco River in southwestern Oregon to southern Monterey County, California, where winter rain and summer fog keep the forest damp year round.
Wild only on the western slope of the Sierra Nevada in California, in some 65 to 75 scattered groves within mixed conifer forest, mostly between about 1,400 and 2,000 m.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across eastern North America, from Cape Breton Island in Nova Scotia to northern Florida, and west to eastern Minnesota and eastern Texas, on rich, moist, well-drained upland soils. In Vermont a tree of mixed hardwood forest.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: A natural hybrid of red and silver maple, found wild where the two meet in eastern North America, mostly on wet bottomland. Most planted trees are named selections of it.
Wild in western and southern Europe, northwest Africa and southwest Asia, mostly as an understory shrub of woods on chalk and limestone.
Wild along the Atlantic and Gulf coastal plain, from southern Maine to Florida and Texas, in swamps, wet woods and along streams.
Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to Georgia, as a small understory tree of moist woods and forest edges. Native to Vermont.
Wild across eastern North America, from Nova Scotia to Minnesota and south to Florida and Texas, in the understory of hardwood forest. Native to Vermont.
Wild across most of Europe and into western Asia, climbing trees, rocks and walls in woodland. In North America it has escaped from gardens and smothers trees and ground in many places.
Wild only in central China, on mountain slopes, in scrub and among rocks between about 300 and 1,300 m. Rare in the wild.
Wild across eastern North America, from Maine and Ontario to Kansas and south to Florida and Texas, in moist, rich woods and along streams.
Its only wild populations are in Sichuan, in southern China; it reached Japan long ago and was grown there for fibre, which is why it was once thought Japanese.
Wild in mountain thickets of Japan, eastern China and Taiwan.
Wild across Europe, northwest Africa and western Asia, in hedges and open woods. Brought to North America as a hedge, it is now invasive in woods across the Northeast and Midwest, Vermont included.
Wild only on rocky hills in the Balkan Peninsula. Grown in Europe since the 1500s and in North America since colonial times, it lingers around old homesites long after the house is gone.

Wild across eastern North America, from Cape Breton Island to Florida and west to the edge of the Great Plains, mostly on moist bottomland and along streams. Dutch elm disease has killed most of the large trees.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across eastern North America, from southern Quebec and Maine to Florida and west to the Dakotas and Texas, on moist, rich soils of slopes and stream banks.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern Maine to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas, often on dry, poor upland soils and ridges.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Maine to Georgia and west to the Ohio Valley, on dry, sandy or gravelly upland ridges and slopes.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southern Maine and New York south along the Appalachians to Georgia, on dry, rocky ridges and upper slopes where few other oaks do well.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The most widespread tree in North America, wild from Newfoundland to Alaska and south in the mountains to Mexico. It springs up after fire and logging and spreads by root suckers into large clones.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across the eastern and central United States and southern Canada, on moist bottomland along rivers, where it is among the fastest-growing native trees.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across Canada and the northern United States, south in the Appalachians; one of the first trees to come up after fire or clearcutting, and short-lived.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The largest native willow, wild across eastern North America on stream banks, floodplains and lake shores, wherever the ground stays wet.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from central Maine to Georgia, on dry, sandy or rocky soils: the pine of the New Jersey Pine Barrens. It can sprout again from the trunk after fire, which few pines can.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from central and southeastern Europe to western Asia, as a small tree of open woods, steppe edges and river valleys.
Wild across eastern North America, from southern Quebec and Ontario to Florida and Texas, in pastures, open woods and thickets.
Wild across much of Europe, from Spain and southern England east to the Black Sea, in mixed woods on rich, often limy soils and on rocky slopes.

Wild in Mongolia, northern China, Korea and Central Asia, on dry plains and steppe. Planted across the American Plains for its hardiness, it has spread into fields and roadsides and is invasive in many states.
Wild in China; despite the name it reached Japan through cultivation. Planted for centuries around temples and along streets in China and Korea.
Wild across Europe and western and central Asia, along rivers and in wet meadows. Brought to North America in colonial times, it has naturalized along streams.
Wild across northern Europe and northern Asia to Japan, in damp woods, along streams and at forest edges.
Wild in Japan, Korea and China in mountain forests. Most planted Japanese cherries are cultivars of it or its hybrids, selected over centuries for their blossom.
Wild in Japan, Korea, China and the Philippines, as a small tree of woodland edges and thickets in hills and low mountains.
Wild in Manchuria, Korea and the Russian Far East, along rivers and in mixed forest. Among the hardiest cherries, which is why it is planted in cold climates.
Wild across the boreal forest of Canada and Alaska and south into the northern United States, Vermont included, on river flats and moist lowland.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Descended from wild pears of Europe and western Asia; the cultivated pear has been grown since ancient times and escapes to hedgerows and old fields.
Wild in the mountains of central and southern Europe and western Asia, in mixed woods. Planted widely in Britain and elsewhere, it has spread far beyond its native range.

Wild in northern and central China and Taiwan. Brought to Philadelphia in 1784 and planted as a city tree, it is now invasive across much of the United States, coming up in cracks, lots and roadsides.
Wild across Europe, southwest Asia and North Africa along rivers, lakes and in wet woods. It has naturalized in the northeastern United States, along streams and in wetlands.
Wild in the Midwest and the Ohio Valley, from western Pennsylvania to Iowa and south to Tennessee, on moist bottomland and along streams.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Vermont and southern Ontario west to Minnesota and south to Tennessee, mostly on moist bottomland soils rich in lime; often treated as a variety of sugar maple.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Iran across southern Asia to China and Korea. Planted for its flowers, it has escaped across the southeastern United States, where it is invasive.
Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south in the Appalachians to Georgia, at woodland edges and in open woods. Native to Vermont.
Wild only in the high southern Appalachians of Virginia, North Carolina and Tennessee, above about 1,500 m, where the balsam woolly adelgid has killed most of the mature trees.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across eastern North America, from southern Quebec and Maine to Georgia and west to Minnesota and Texas, on upland slopes and in bottomland woods. Native to Vermont, mostly in the Champlain Valley.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the eastern United States, from western New York and southern Ontario to Florida and west to Nebraska and Texas, in the shady understory of rich bottomland woods, often in patches from root suckers.
The most widespread hickory, wild from southern Quebec and New England to Florida and west to Minnesota and Texas, in moist bottomland and on rich slopes.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in a small area of the Gulf states (Georgia, Florida, Alabama and Mississippi) along streams; planted and naturalized far beyond.
Wild in the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas and Kansas, mostly on bottomland along rivers.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern New England and Ontario to Florida and west to Illinois and Texas, mostly on dry ridges and upland slopes in oak-hickory forest.
Wild in China, Korea and Taiwan in mountain forests. Resistant to chestnut blight, it has been crossed with American chestnut in the effort to bring that tree back.

Wild from New Brunswick and southern Quebec to Minnesota and south to Arkansas and Georgia, on rich, well-drained soils of slopes and stream terraces. Native to Vermont; butternut canker has killed most of the wild trees.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Connecticut and southern New York to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, in old fields, open woods and bottomland.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from coastal Massachusetts to Florida and west to Missouri and Texas, in the understory of moist mixed woods and on coastal dunes.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Native from the Balkans east through Central Asia to the Himalayas and southwest China, in mountain forests; grown for its nuts since ancient times.
Wild across Europe and western Asia, as an understory shrub of woods and hedgerows, long coppiced for poles and grown for its nuts.
Endemic to Japan, in mountain forests; planted around temples and shrines for centuries and grown widely for timber in Japan and China.
Wild across most of Europe, from Ireland to the Caucasus, in mixed woods on moist, rich soils. Ash dieback, a fungal disease, has killed much of it since the 1990s.
Wild in a few scattered places in the southern United States (Tennessee, Alabama, the Ozarks and the Edwards Plateau of Texas), on limestone bluffs and rocky glades. Rare in the wild.

Wild across the boreal forest from Newfoundland to Alaska and south into the northern United States, Vermont included, mostly in bogs and swamps; the one conifer of the region that drops its needles each fall.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The most widespread conifer of the eastern United States, wild from Maine and southern Ontario to Florida and west to the Plains, in old fields, on dry rocky ground and limestone. It spreads quickly into abandoned pasture.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild originally only in the Red River country of Oklahoma, Texas and Arkansas, in bottomland. Planted across the Plains as thorny living fences before barbed wire, it has naturalized far beyond.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: The hardiest native magnolia, wild from western New York and southern Ontario south through the Appalachians to Georgia and west to the Ozarks, on rich, moist slopes.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from southwestern Pennsylvania south through the Appalachians to northern Florida and west to Louisiana, on well-drained slopes in oak and pine woods.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild across the eastern United States, from southern New England and Ontario to Florida and Texas, on moist bottomland and lower slopes. It hybridizes readily with the introduced white mulberry.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild in the Appalachians and the Ozarks, from southern Pennsylvania to Georgia and Arkansas, in the understory of rich, moist woods and ravines.
Wild in China and Korea, on dry hillsides and in open woods. Planted widely as a street tree, it seeds itself freely and is invasive in some southern states.

Wild from Nova Scotia and southern Quebec through New England and New York, and south along the high Appalachians to North Carolina, on cool, moist mountain slopes. In Vermont it is the spruce of the Green Mountains.
source: Silvics of North America (U.S. Forest Service)

habitat: Wild from Spain and North Africa across central and southern Europe to Central Asia, along rivers and on damp ground. Planted in North America since colonial times, it spreads by root suckers and is invasive in many states.
Wild across the southeastern and central United States, from southern New England to Florida and west to Kansas and Texas, on dry, poor, rocky or sandy uplands.
Domesticated in China several thousand years ago from wild trees of northwest China; the name persica comes from its arrival in Europe by way of Persia.
Wild in northern China, along rivers. It reached Europe and the Americas by the 1700s; most weeping willows planted in the North are its hardier hybrids.
Wild across eastern Asia, from the Himalayas to China, Korea and Japan, in hill forests. Planted in the eastern United States for wildlife, it has escaped in places.
Wild in southeastern Europe and western Asia, from the Balkans to the Caucasus and Central Asia, in thickets and woodland edges. Its purple-leaved selections are common street trees.
Wild only in a small area of Alabama, Georgia and South Carolina, in the understory of moist, rich woods along streams.
Wild across the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Texas, in the understory of moist woods and along streams.
Wild across eastern North America, from Newfoundland to Minnesota and south to the Appalachians, in bogs, wet woods and on dry rocky ground. Native to Vermont.
Wild in Japan and eastern China. Planted widely as a hedge, it has spread through woods across the Northeast, Vermont included, and is banned from sale in several states as invasive.
Wild in the southeastern United States, from Virginia to Florida and west to Mississippi, in moist woods, along streams and on wooded hillsides.
Wild across eastern and southern North America, from Nova Scotia to Florida and west to California, in swamps, along pond edges and streams, often standing in water. Native to Vermont.
Wild in Siberia, Mongolia and northern China, on dry steppe and river banks. Planted across the Canadian Prairies for shelterbelts, it has escaped in places.
Wild across northeastern North America, from Maine and southern Quebec to Minnesota and south to Virginia and Oklahoma, in thickets, old fields and along woodland edges. Native to Vermont.
Wild across most of northern North America, from Newfoundland to Alaska and south in the mountains, in wet thickets, along streams and in swamps. Native to Vermont.
Wild across northeastern North America, from Newfoundland to Saskatchewan and south in the Appalachians, on dry, rocky ground and in open woods. Native to Vermont.
